interactive.title: Equal ratios, equal areas
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens on one pV diagram, as in Calculus fundamentals: pressure p in kPa up the side, from 0 to 450, and volume V in m³ along the bottom, from 0 to 0.8. On it is the curve p = 40 ÷ V, a gas held at a steady temperature, so p × V stays at 40 all along it: 400 kPa at 0.1 m³, 200 at 0.2, 100 at 0.4 and 50 at 0.8. Two handles on the bottom axis mark the start volume V₁ and the end volume V₂; each drags from 0.1 to 0.8 m³ in steps of 0.05, and a dot on the curve above each shows its pressure. Between them stand bars of equal width, as in Calculus fundamentals lesson 8, each as tall as the curve at its middle, so each bar is a pressure times a change in volume, a little work; a kPa times a m³ is a kJ. Buttons under the graph set how many bars stand there: 4, 8 or 100. The readouts give the bars' total and, from screen 6, C × ln(V₂ ÷ V₁) worked with the ln key, where C = 40, both in kJ. A 'Double it' button moves V₂ to twice V₁ (while squeezing it reads 'Halve it', and the squeeze ends at half the start volume); it is greyed out while V₁ is over 0.4 m³, where twice V₁ would run off the axis. A switch, 'Squeeze it', swaps the two handles, so the gas runs from the larger volume back to the smaller: each bar's width, the change in volume, is then minus, the bars are hatched and both readouts turn minus. A second switch, 'Show n = 1.3', lays a second curve from the same start point, one where p × V^1.3 stays the same, an example polytropic process, with the area under it outlined and a third readout, its work from (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂) ÷ (n − 1), the rule from Calculus fundamentals lesson 9; while it is on, the pressure axis stretches to 800 kPa so that curve fits. The rule: here pV = C, so p = C ÷ V, and the work is the area under that curve between V₁ and V₂. Doubling the volume makes each bar twice as wide and, at twice the volume, half as tall, so each bar's area and the bars' total stay the same: the area depends only on V₂ ÷ V₁. Each stretch of the volume by e, about 2.718, adds exactly C, so the area is C × ln(V₂ ÷ V₁), where ln is the natural log from lesson 4 and C = p₁V₁. Screen by screen: 1 writes pV = C beside the curve, with 4 bars standing from the start, then the old rule (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂) ÷ (n − 1) with n = 1, which gives (40 − 40) ÷ 0, and the reverse power rule's step for 40 × V⁻¹, add one to the power to get V⁰, then divide by 0, struck through; then the bars from 0.1 to 0.2 m³ go from 4 (27.65 kJ) to 8 (27.71 kJ) to 100 (27.73 kJ). 2 asks why the reverse power rule cannot find this area: p = 40 × V⁻¹, and adding one to the power −1 gives 0, a division by 0; not 'the curve never meets the axis, so the area is endless' (the bars stop at V₂ and settle on 27.73 kJ) or 'pV = C is a straight line, so no area rule is needed' (p halves as V doubles, so the line bends). 3 asks what the bars from 0.2 to 0.4 m³ total, given 27.73 kJ from 0.1 to 0.2: 27.73 kJ, not 55.45 kJ (twice as wide, but the pressure is half) or 13.86 kJ (half the pressure, but the stretch is twice as wide). 4 shows why: the bars from 0.2 to 0.4 m³ are drawn beside those from 0.1 to 0.2, each twice as wide and half as tall as its partner, and one pair is lifted and laid over the other to show the same area; then 'Double it' runs from 0.15 to 0.3 and from 0.3 to 0.6 m³, 27.73 kJ each time, and 0.1 to 0.4 m³, two doublings, gives 55.45 kJ. 5 asks for the work from 0.1 to 0.8 m³: 83.18 kJ (0.8 ÷ 0.1 = 8 = 2 × 2 × 2, three doublings), not 194.08 kJ (seven steps of 0.1 m³, as if the work went by the difference) or 221.81 kJ (eight doublings, the ratio 8 taken as the count). 6 finds the stretch that adds exactly C: buttons cut the stretch from 0.1 m³ into 1, 2, 4, 12 and 365 bars, each as wide as one part of the volume where it starts and as tall as the curve at its left edge, so each bar's area is 40 ÷ parts and together they make 40 kJ every time; the last bar ends at 0.2, 0.225, 0.244, 0.261 and 0.271 m³, lesson 2's (1 + 1/parts)^parts times 0.1, settling on e × 0.1 ≈ 0.272 m³. Each bar's left edge is its tallest point, so the bars stand a little above the curve, by less as they thin, the overshoot, measured against 100 mid-height bars up to the last bar's end, shrinking towards nothing: the area from V₁ to e × V₁ is exactly C. Each further stretch by e adds another C, so the work is C times the number of e-stretches, ln(V₂ ÷ V₁), lesson 4's power you need; then the second readout appears: 40 × ln 2 = 40 × 0.693 = 27.73 kJ, the bars' total. 7 asks for the work from 0.1 to 0.3 m³: 43.94 kJ (40 × ln 3 = 40 × 1.099), not 19.08 kJ (40 × log 3, the log key, which counts ten-fold stretches) or −64.38 kJ (40 × ln 0.2, the difference 0.3 − 0.1 put where the ratio belongs). 8 flips 'Squeeze it' with V₁ = 0.2 and V₂ = 0.1 m³: the pressure climbs from 200 to 400 kPa, V₂ ÷ V₁ = 0.5, the same as 200 ÷ 400, and both readouts read −27.73 kJ: the gas does −27.73 kJ of work, so the piston does 27.73 kJ on it. 9 asks for the gas's work squeezed from 0.4 to 0.1 m³: −55.45 kJ (40 × ln 0.25), not +55.45 kJ (a ratio below 1 has a minus ln, as every bar's width is minus) or 0 kJ (pV is 40 at both ends, but the work is the area under the curve, not the change in pV). 10 flips 'Show n = 1.3' on the expansion from 0.1 to 0.2 m³: the new curve falls to 162 kPa at 0.2 m³, below the isothermal 200, because p × V^1.3 staying the same makes pV = C ÷ V^0.3, which shrinks as V grows (32.49 at 0.2 m³ against 40); its work is (40 − 32.49) ÷ 0.3 = 25.03 kJ against 27.73 kJ. 11 asks, squeezing from 0.2 m³ at 200 kPa to the same end volume of 0.1 m³, which curve takes less work: the isothermal, 27.73 kJ against 30.82 kJ, because the n = 1.3 curve climbs to 492 kPa, above the isothermal 400, as pV = C ÷ V^0.3 grows when V shrinks; not the n = 1.3 curve (it gave less work expanding, but squeezing runs its pV the other way) or 'the same, since both end at 0.1 m³' (the work is the area under the path, not set by its ends). 12 and 13 redraw the curve and axes for their own gas and mix it all. 12: gas at 300 kPa in 0.1 m³ expands at a steady temperature to 0.5 m³: 48.28 kJ (C = 30, 30 × ln 5 = 30 × 1.609), not 20.97 kJ (30 × log 5) or 482.83 kJ (300 × ln 5, with V₁ left out of C = p₁V₁). 13: say an air compressor squeezes 0.08 m³ of air at 100 kPa to 800 kPa at a steady temperature: −16.64 kJ (pV stays 8, so V₂ ÷ V₁ = 100 ÷ 800 = 1/8, and 8 × ln(1/8) = 8 × −2.079), not −7.22 kJ (8 × log(1/8), the log key) or +16.64 kJ (the minus lost, though squeezing makes the ratio below 1). 14, a preview, puts the curve y = 1 ÷ x on fresh axes, x from 0 to 4, shaded from 1 to a dragged x, so the shaded area is C × ln(x ÷ 1) with C = 1, which is ln x; one more thin bar of width h at x adds about h × 1 ÷ x, so ln x climbs at a rate of 1 ÷ x: the slope of ln x is 1 ÷ x, which the Derivatives course takes up. A puzzle offers its three answers, and a wrong pick gets a one-line hint showing where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The gas is ideal and its temperature held exactly steady. Holding it steady needs heat to flow into the gas as it expands and out as it is squeezed, so a real gas comes near the isothermal curve only when the process is slow or the gas well cooled. The value 1.3 is an example, not a measured one. The bars take the pressure at their middles, so a few bars come out a little under the exact area. Readouts are rounded to two decimal places, so a total can differ from the ln rule in the last figure.

explain.text:
When a gas expands while its temperature holds steady, its pressure falls in step with its volume, and the work it does is W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁). The log is there because, along the curve such a gas follows, every doubling of the volume adds the same work, wherever it starts.

Keep a gas at one temperature and squeeze it or let it expand, and its pressure and volume change so that pV stays the same, which is Boyle's law.[^2] That is pVⁿ = C from Calculus fundamentals with n = 1, and the process is called [[isothermal]], meaning at a steady temperature.[^3] There the area under pVⁿ = C came out as (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂) ÷ (n − 1). Here pV is the same at both ends, so that rule gives 0 ÷ 0. The reason is underneath it: p = C ÷ V is C × V⁻¹, and the reverse power rule adds one to the power, giving V⁰, then divides by the new power, 0, which cannot be done.[^4] The area is still there, so count it with bars, as in Calculus fundamentals. Say the gas starts at 400 kPa in 0.1 m³, so C = 400 × 0.1 = 40 kJ, since a kPa times a m³ is a kJ, as in Calculus fundamentals, and along p = 40 ÷ V it falls to 200 kPa at 0.2 m³. Four mid-height bars from 0.1 to 0.2 m³ total 27.65 kJ, and a hundred total 27.73 kJ. Now double again, from 0.2 to 0.4 m³. Each bar there is twice as wide, because the stretch is twice as long, and half as tall, because at twice the volume 40 ÷ V is half the pressure. Twice the width times half the height is the same area, so the total is 27.73 kJ again. The same pairing works from any start, so the work depends only on V₂ ÷ V₁: from 0.1 to 0.8 m³ is a ratio of 8, three doublings, 3 × 27.73 = 83.18 kJ, not seven times 27.73 for seven steps of 0.1 m³.

Counting doublings is a log, as in lesson 4: log₂ 8 = 3. The natural log comes from asking which stretch adds exactly C. Cut the stretch from V₁ into bars, each as wide as one part in k of the volume where it starts, V ÷ k, and as tall as the curve at its left edge, C ÷ V. Each bar's area is then (V ÷ k) × (C ÷ V) = C ÷ k, whatever V is, so k bars make exactly C. Each bar ends (1 + 1/k) times as far along as it starts, so the last ends at (1 + 1/k)ᵏ × V₁, lesson 2's sum with k parts, which settles on e, about 2.718,[^1] as k grows. A bar's left edge is its tallest point, so the bars stand a little above the curve, by less as they thin, the overshoot shrinking towards nothing, so the area from V₁ to e × V₁ is exactly C. Each further stretch by e adds another C, so the area is C times the number of e-stretches from V₁ to V₂, and the power of e that makes V₂ ÷ V₁ is its natural log, ln.[^5] With C = p₁V₁, W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁). Check it on the bars: 40 × ln 2 = 40 × 0.693 = 27.73 kJ. It has to be the ln key: 40 × log 2 = 12.04 counts ten-fold stretches, not e-fold ones. Engineering notes write the steady pV as p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ = mRT,[^3] and physics notes give the work of a slow, steady-temperature expansion as nRT ln(V₂/V₁),[^6] their nRT being the same pV, with n there counting the gas in moles, not a power.

Squeeze the gas instead and every change in volume is minus: from 0.2 back to 0.1 m³, V₂ ÷ V₁ = 0.5 and 40 × ln 0.5 = −27.73 kJ, so the piston does 27.73 kJ of work on the gas. Lay a curve with n = 1.3, an example value, from the same start: p × V^1.3 staying the same makes pV = C ÷ V^0.3, which shrinks as the gas expands and grows as it is squeezed. So expanding from 0.1 to 0.2 m³ that gas does 25.03 kJ against 27.73, and a squeeze that starts at 200 kPa in 0.2 m³ takes 30.82 kJ on the n = 1.3 curve against 27.73 on the steady one, to the same end volume of 0.1 m³: to that end volume, the steady-temperature squeeze takes less work. All of this is a simplified model of an ideal gas: holding the temperature steady needs heat to flow in as the gas expands and out as it is squeezed, so a real process comes near it only when it is slow or well cooled. The course's capacitor follows the same pattern: it takes 10 s to halve from 400 V or from 100 V, and the log counts the halvings as it counts the stretches here. **A gas expanding at a steady temperature keeps pV the same, and the work it does, the area under p = C ÷ V, is W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁),[^6] the same for every doubling of its volume and minus when it is squeezed.**

analogy.text: Resistors come in the E12 series: twelve values in every × 10, from 10, 12, 15 and so on up to 82 ohms, then 100,[^7] each about 1.2 times the last. From 10 to 100 ohms is twelve steps, and so is 100 to 1000: the count depends only on how many times bigger the top value is, not on how far apart the two are. Work under p = C ÷ V counts the same way: equal ratios of volume, equal work.
analogy.breaks: The E12 values are rounded, so their steps are only roughly equal ratios, and the count goes in whole steps, while the area under the curve grows smoothly and every stretch by the same ratio adds exactly the same work. And every decade holds twelve values, while the work for one doubling grows with C: a gas with twice the pV does twice the work.

practice.text:
- Check the process is isothermal: the temperature holds steady, so pV is the same at both ends. If it follows pVⁿ = C with n not 1, use (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂) ÷ (n − 1) instead.
- Work out C = p₁V₁. In kPa and m³ it comes out in kJ.
- Find the ratio V₂ ÷ V₁. Given pressures instead, use p₁ ÷ p₂: when pV stays the same, the volume ratio is the pressure ratio upside down.
- Press ln on the ratio, not log.
- Multiply: W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁).
- Check the sign: plus as the gas expands, minus as it is squeezed, when the piston does the work on the gas.

**Rule of thumb:** each doubling of the volume adds 0.693 × p₁V₁, and each stretch by e, about 2.718, adds p₁V₁ itself.

**Worked example:** Say an air compressor squeezes 0.08 m³ of air at 100 kPa to 800 kPa, with its temperature held steady. C = 100 × 0.08 = 8 kJ. pV stays at 8, so the air ends at 8 ÷ 800 = 0.01 m³, and V₂ ÷ V₁ = 0.01 ÷ 0.08 = 1/8, the same as 100 ÷ 800. ln(1/8) = −2.079, so W = 8 × −2.079 = −16.64 kJ: the air does −16.64 kJ of work, which means the piston does 16.64 kJ on it. Check by halvings: 1/8 is three halvings, and 3 × 0.6931 × 8 ≈ 16.64 kJ.

**Common mistakes**
- Pressing log instead of ln: 8 × log(1/8) = −7.22 kJ counts ten-fold stretches, not e-fold ones.
- Using the difference V₂ − V₁ where the ratio belongs: equal ratios, not equal gaps, give equal work.
- Leaving V₁ out of C: it is p₁V₁, not p₁.
- Losing the minus on a squeeze.
- Putting n = 1 into (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂) ÷ (n − 1): it gives 0 ÷ 0.
- Mixing units: bar times litres gives hundreds of joules, since 1 bar = 100 kPa[^8] and 1 bar × 1 litre = 100 J, not kJ.
